items.text: Dick's Bar in New York was where Merritt wrote much of its 69 love songs, and he said he spent eight hours a day there.
items.why: "Merritt wrote much of the album at Dick's Bar in New York, saying that he was 'literally there eight hours a day, writing'".

items.text: 7 September 1999
items.why: Infobox "Released: September 7, 1999".

items.text: April 1999 at Polar West, Mother West, Polar Mother and Sonics
items.why: Infobox "Recorded: April 1999" and "Studios: Polar West, Mother West, Polar Mother, and Sonics".

items.text: Stephin Merritt
items.why: Infobox "Producer: Stephin Merritt".

items.text: Merge
items.why: Infobox "Label: Merge".

items.text: In the first plan, four drag queens would star in a theatre revue, and the one the crowd liked most by the end of the evening would be paid.
items.why: "I'd have a theatrical revue with four drag queens. And whoever the audience liked best at the end of the night would get paid."

items.text: In a gay piano bar in Manhattan, Merritt heard a pianist play Stephen Sondheim songs and decided to move into theatre music.
items.why: "sitting in a gay piano bar in Manhattan, listening to the pianist's interpretations of Stephen Sondheim songs, when he decided he ought to get into theatre music".

items.text: He began with one hundred love songs, a way of introducing himself to the world.
items.why: Pack: "I decided I'd write one hundred love songs". He planned a hundred; "began with" suggests he started writing them.

items.text: Working out how long that would take, he settled on sixty-nine.
items.why: Pack: "Then I realized how long that would be. So I settled on sixty-nine." That is the length of the work, not "how long that would take" to write.

items.text: He had read about Charles Ives's 114 Songs that day and thought he could do something similar.
items.why: "inspiration in Charles Ives' 114 Songs, about which he had read earlier in the day ... I could do something like that".

items.text: Fleetwood Mac, Billie Holiday and Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark were other influences.
items.why: "Other influences on 69 Love Songs included Fleetwood Mac, Billie Holiday and Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark".

items.text: Merritt wrote all 69 songs.
items.why: Lead: "69 love songs, all written by Magnetic Fields frontman Stephin Merritt".

items.text: He also produced and engineered the record, with five other people on engineering and Jeff Lipton on mastering.
items.why: Production: Merritt "production, engineering"; five others on engineering (Berman, Ewen, Gonson, Masunaga, Newman); "Jeff Lipton – mastering".

items.text: Recording happened in April 1999 at four studios: Polar West, Mother West, Polar Mother and Sonics.
items.why: Infobox "Recorded: April 1999", four studios listed (repeats the fact row).

items.text: Shirley Simms sang on several songs, and Dudley Klute took lead vocals on six.
items.why: Simms: duet on one song plus vocals on six; Klute: lead vocals on six listed songs.

items.text: Sam Davol played cello and flute, and Daniel Handler added accordion and keyboards.
items.why: "Sam Davol – cello, flute"; "Daniel Handler – accordion, keyboards, arrangement on 'Asleep and Dreaming'".

items.text: In May 2000 Circus released it in Europe and Australia, without the booklet.
items.why: "On May 29, 2000, the album was released by Circus ... in Europe and Australia without the booklet insert".

items.text: In April 2010 Merge issued a limited vinyl edition of 1,000 copies.
items.why: "On April 20, 2010, Merge released a limited edition 6×10\" vinyl version limited to 1,000 copies".

items.text: In December 2006 LD Beghtol published a book on the album in Continuum's 33 1/3 series.
items.why: "LD Beghtol's explication ... released on December 15, 2006, by Continuum ... as part of their 33 1/3 series" (Beghtol wrote it, Continuum published it).

items.text: The band played all 69 songs in order seven times, five in America and two in London.
items.why: "On seven occasions (five in the United States and two in London ...) the Magnetic Fields performed all 69 love songs, in order, over two nights".

items.text: Peter Gabriel covered "The Book of Love", and Superchunk covered "I Don't Want to Get Over You" in 2025.
items.why: "'The Book of Love' was covered by Peter Gabriel"; "'I Don't Want to Get Over You' was covered by Superchunk in 2025".

items.text: Claudia Gonson takes the lead vocal on it.
items.why: Claudia Gonson: "lead vocals on 'Reno Dakota'".

items.where: listen_for:Time Enough for Rocking When We're Old
items.text: John Woo plays banjo, lead guitar, mandolin and bass on it.
items.why: Pack: "John Woo – banjo, lead guitar, mandolin, bass on 'Time Enough for Rocking When We're Old'". Read naturally, the song is attached only to bass; the note puts all four instruments on that track.

items.text: Chris Ewen plays theremin on it, and Dudley Klute sings lead.
items.why: "Chris Ewen ... theremin on 'Blue You'"; Dudley Klute lead vocals list includes "Blue You".

items.text: Shirley Simms sings a duet with Merritt on it.
items.why: "Shirley Simms – duet with Merritt on 'Papa Was a Rodeo'".

missed: What the songs are like: Merritt's line that it is "not remotely an album about love. It's an album about love songs", the spread of genres (country, synth-pop, free jazz, mournful ballads) and the lyrics about straight, gay and bisexual relationships. Also "Yeah! Oh, Yeah!", the Gonson and Merritt duet about a husband murdering his wife, which would make a strong listen_for item.
